newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algerian rebels kill 51 civilians - newspapers.
newsitem.headline: Algerian rebels kill 51 civilians - newspapers.

text.p: Suspected Moslem rebels have killed 51 civilians, including a baby and 12 women, in Algeria in the latest surge of violence reported by Algerian newspapers on Tuesday.

The civilians died in four attacks -- the latest at the weekend -- in Algiers and the neighbouring province of Medea, showing no letup in the killing since the country's multi-party general election was held last month.
Around 300 people have died since the ballot, according to Algerian newspaper reports.
On Saturday night, rebels killed 27 people, including 12 women, in a raid in Benia village in Medea province, 70 km (45 miles) south of Algiers, El Watan newspaper said.

The slaughter followed an attack earlier in the week on another hamlet, Ouzera, in Medea when guerrillas killed 18 villagers, said the French-language newspaper, normally well informed on security issues.
On Saturday, as Algeria was marking its 35th Independence Day anniversary, a bomb exploded in Ouzera cemetery where the 18 had been buried, killing three boy scouts, said El Watan.
The newspaper said the same rebels who killed the 18 villagers had planted the bomb.
In Algiers, rebels cut the throats of three soccer fans caught at fake roadblock near Jenane Hassan on the northern edge of the capital, said Liberte newspaper.
The three young men were among tens of thousands of people who took to Algiers streets to celebrate Union Algiers soccer team who won the country's premier football cup on Saturday, Liberte said.

Algerian newspapers, tightly controlled on security issues and violence, have now reported about 300 civilians being killed by Moslem rebels since June 5 general election. At least a dozen young girls have also been kidnapped in that time, apparently to serve as "temporary brides" for the guerrillas.

The authorities saw the June ballot as a key step towards bringing the North African country out of more than five years of violence. It plunged into conflict after the authorities in January 1992 cancelled a general election whose first round was dominated by the Islamic Salvation Front (FIS).

On Monday, an Algiers court sentenced FIS leader Abdelkader Hachani to five years' imprisonment for trying to undermine state security just after that election was scrapped. He was expected to be freed later on Tuesday after having spent more than five years in preventative detention.

President Liamine Zeroual barred radical Islamists from the June general election but allowed moderate Islamists to compete as part of his strategy to restore peace to the country in which about 60,000 people have been killed in under six years.
Two Islamist-leaning parties won a total of 103 seats in the 380-member National Assembly (lower house).
Seven Moslem fundamentalists are members of a three-party coalition government of 38 ministers or secretaries of state.
